services.title: Personal Injury
services.text: When you suffer an injury because of someone else's negligence, you deserve to be compensated. Don't put yourself in financial peril because of someone else's carelessness.
services.lead: If you have been injured due to someone else's negligence, you deserve experienced legal representation and the chance to recover fair compensation. The firm serves injury victims across Pasadena and the greater Houston area, and takes injury calls 24 hours a day for a free consultation.

covers.title: Car, truck and motorcycle accidents
covers.text: Collisions on I-45, Loop 610, Beltway 8 and local roads, including 18-wheelers, delivery vehicles and crashes caused by drivers who had been drinking.

covers.title: Pedestrian, bicycle, boating and aviation accidents
covers.text: Walkers, runners, cyclists, and people hurt on the water or in the air by someone else's negligence.

covers.title: Dangerous property and defective products
covers.text: Slip and fall and premises liability claims, construction site accidents, and injuries caused by defective products.

covers.title: Medical malpractice and nursing home neglect
covers.text: Claims arising from medical negligence, including medication errors, and from the neglect or abuse of elderly residents in care facilities.

covers.title: Wrongful death
covers.text: Representing families who have lost a loved one because of someone else's negligence.

covers.title: Assault, battery and abuse claims
covers.text: Civil litigation on behalf of victims of intentional harm, including sexual assault and abuse.

questions.q: What does a personal injury consultation cost?
questions.a: The initial consultation is free and carries no obligation, and we work on a contingency fee basis, so you pay nothing unless we win your case. You can call 24/7, and if we are not available immediately we will respond to your inquiry as soon as possible.

questions.q: How long do I have to file a claim in Texas?
questions.a: Generally you have two years from the date of the injury to file a claim, and certain claims have shorter deadlines.

questions.q: How long will my case take?
questions.a: Many cases resolve in 12 to 18 months, but more complex cases can take longer. Most personal injury claims settle out of court, and we are ready to take your case to trial if a fair settlement is not offered.

questions.q: Will you help me find medical care?
questions.a: Yes. Part of the firm's full-service approach is helping you find local medical specialists while your claim is handled.

questions.q: I feel fine after the crash. Should I still see a doctor?
questions.a: See a doctor anyway. Some injuries show no symptoms right away, and a gap in treatment is used against you later.

questions.q: Should I talk to my own insurance company?
questions.a: Yes, but keep the conversation brief. Do not give a recorded statement or discuss settlement terms without legal advice.

questions.q: Can I post about the accident on social media?
questions.a: Stay offline about the accident until the case is resolved. Posts are used as evidence against injured people.

questions.q: What mistakes should I avoid?
questions.a: Talking to adjusters or posting on social media, ignoring the treatment plan your doctor set, accepting a settlement too soon, and going back to work before you are medically cleared.

questions.q: Should I settle or go to trial?
questions.a: That depends on your case. You get honest advice about whether to settle or take the case to trial, and a strategy built around your own circumstances.

services.title: Estate Planning
services.summary: Wills, trusts, directives and powers of attorney.
services.text: Estate planning and family protection are essential steps in ensuring that your loved ones are cared for and your wishes are honored.
services.lead: Attorney Michael West is the principal attorney at West & West, LLP, and helps individuals and families throughout the greater Houston area with estate planning, probate, guardianship, elder law and related matters. He believes clients make better decisions when they understand the law, which is why education is an important part of every consultation.

covers.title: Last will and testament
covers.text: Drafting and updating wills so your estate is distributed according to your intentions.

covers.title: Trusts
covers.text: Revocable living trusts, and irrevocable trusts where they fit your plan.

covers.title: Powers of attorney
covers.text: Durable financial and medical powers of attorney naming people you trust to decide for you.

covers.title: Advance directives
covers.text: Directive to physicians, healthcare proxies and HIPAA authorizations so your medical preferences are known and respected.

covers.title: Guardianship designations
covers.text: A declaration of guardian naming the person you would want to raise your minor children or care for you.

covers.title: Digital assets
covers.text: Planning for cryptocurrency, social media accounts, cloud storage, reward programs and subscription services.

covers.title: Beneficiary and business succession review
covers.text: Checking beneficiary designations and planning the future ownership and management of a business you own.

questions.q: Is estate planning only for wealthy people?
questions.a: No. Almost every adult benefits from a plan. If you own a home, have children, hold retirement accounts, run a business, or want someone you trust to make healthcare decisions for you, estate planning belongs in your financial and legal planning.

questions.q: I already have a will. Do I need an estate plan?
questions.a: A will is only one piece of the puzzle. A complete plan also covers decisions made during your lifetime if you become unable to make them yourself.

questions.q: What happens if I do not have a plan?
questions.a: Important financial and medical decisions may be left to the courts or decided by state law rather than by your own wishes. Under the Texas Estates Code, property passes to a surviving spouse, then children or descendants, then parents, then brothers and sisters, then other relatives.

questions.q: What is the difference between a will and a trust?
questions.a: A will takes effect at death and generally goes through probate. A trust can own assets during your lifetime, and assets properly transferred into a revocable living trust may avoid probate.

questions.q: Does estate planning include healthcare decisions?
questions.a: Yes. Medical powers of attorney, a directive to physicians and family or surrogates, and HIPAA authorizations are part of a complete plan.

questions.q: How often should I update my plan?
questions.a: After any major life event, and otherwise reviewing your estate plan every three to five years is a good practice.

questions.q: What should I bring to a consultation?
questions.a: A list of your assets, existing wills or trusts, retirement account information, life insurance policies, beneficiary designations, business ownership information, and your questions or concerns. You do not need to have everything organized before scheduling a consultation.

questions.q: When is the right time to start?
questions.a: Before a crisis. Creating a plan ahead of time lets you make thoughtful decisions rather than rushed ones, and gives your family clear legal guidance.

services.title: Wills
services.summary: Drafting and updating a Texas will.
services.text: Drafting and updating wills to ensure your estate is distributed according to your intentions, and naming a guardian for minor children.
services.lead: A will sets out who receives your property and who you want to raise your children. A properly prepared will can also simplify probate later by clearly expressing your wishes.

covers.title: A will that is valid in Texas
covers.text: Texas requires that you have legal capacity, that the will is made voluntarily, and that it is properly signed and witnessed by qualified individuals.

covers.title: Self-proving affidavit
covers.text: Without one, your witnesses may need to testify or provide further evidence when the will is offered for probate.

covers.title: Executors and alternates
covers.text: Naming the person who will administer your estate, and one or more alternates in case they cannot serve.

covers.title: Guardian for minor children
covers.text: Naming the person you would want to raise your children if you could not.

covers.title: Property a will can cover
covers.text: Family heirlooms, collectibles, firearms, pets, mineral interests and digital assets, as well as the home and accounts.

questions.q: Do I really need a will if I do not have many assets?
questions.a: Yes. A will names who inherits, who administers your estate and who would raise your children, whatever the size of the estate.

questions.q: Can I write my own will in Texas?
questions.a: Texas recognizes handwritten, or holographic, wills in limited circumstances, but they carry a real risk of errors and ambiguity that surface only after you are gone.

questions.q: Does a will avoid probate?
questions.a: No. A will directs the probate process rather than avoiding it. A funded trust and beneficiary designations are what can keep assets out of probate.

questions.q: Can I change my will after it has been signed?
questions.a: Yes, as long as you have legal capacity.

questions.q: Can I leave someone out of my will?
questions.a: Generally yes, subject to certain legal limitations.

questions.q: Should married couples have separate wills?
questions.a: Each spouse usually signs their own will within one coordinated plan.

questions.q: How often should I review my will?
questions.a: Every three to five years, and after any major change in your family or property.

services.title: Trusts
services.summary: Revocable, irrevocable and special needs trusts.
services.text: Creating and managing revocable, irrevocable and special-purpose trusts for asset protection and legacy planning.
services.lead: A trust can keep assets out of probate, set terms for how and when loved ones receive them, and protect benefits for a family member with disabilities through a special needs trust. The firm works with individuals, families, retirees, business owners and professionals.

covers.title: Revocable living trusts
covers.text: Managing your assets during your lifetime, directing them if you become incapacitated, and passing them on at death.

covers.title: Funding the trust
covers.text: Transferring the home, vacation property, commercial real estate, brokerage accounts, collections, jewelry, artwork and certain intellectual property interests into the trust, because a trust that is never funded does nothing.

covers.title: Pour-over will
covers.text: A will that directs anything left outside the trust into it, so nothing is stranded.

covers.title: Beneficiary designations
covers.text: Retirement accounts and life insurance policies usually call for careful beneficiary planning rather than a direct transfer into the trust.

covers.title: Privacy
covers.text: Trust administration is generally not part of the public probate record.

covers.title: Trusts for children and special needs
covers.text: Terms for how and when children receive what you leave them, and trust documents for a beneficiary with special needs.

questions.q: Can I serve as my own trustee?
questions.a: Yes. Most people serve as the initial trustee of their own revocable living trust and name a successor trustee to step in later.

questions.q: Can I change my living trust?
questions.a: In most cases yes, as long as you have legal capacity. Creating a trust does not mean losing control of your assets.

questions.q: Does a living trust replace my will?
questions.a: Not usually. A pour-over will works alongside the trust and directs any assets you did not transfer into it.

questions.q: Will all of my assets automatically become part of my trust?
questions.a: No. Each asset has to be funded into the trust, and newly acquired property has to be transferred in as well.

questions.q: Can a trust help if I become incapacitated?
questions.a: Yes. Your successor trustee can manage the trust assets without a court proceeding.

questions.q: Is a living trust only for wealthy families?
questions.a: No, and a trust does not eliminate every probate issue either. Whether one fits depends on what you own and what you want to happen.

questions.q: Should my home be placed in a revocable living trust?
questions.a: Often it is appropriate, but it depends on the type of property and any existing loans against it.

services.title: Probate
services.summary: Settling a Texas estate after a loss.
services.text: It's an unfortunate reality of life that everyone dies. If you want to ensure that your estate is maintained, proper estate planning and wills are a necessity.
services.lead: Attorney Michael West helps families through the Texas probate process with compassion, clarity and practical guidance, whether your loved one left a valid will or passed away without one. Clients work directly with him, not through a series of case managers or call centers.

covers.title: Filing the probate application
covers.text: Applying to the right Texas probate court to recognize the will, if there is one, and appoint the person who will administer the estate.

covers.title: Independent and dependent administration
covers.text: Texas strongly favors independent administration, where the executor acts without court approval for every step, which means lower legal costs, faster administration and greater flexibility. A dependent administration needs court approval before selling property, paying certain claims or distributing assets.

covers.title: Muniment of title, heirship and small estates
covers.text: Muniment of title proceedings, determination of heirship, affidavits of heirship and small estate affidavits, where those simpler routes are available.

covers.title: Executors and administrators
covers.text: Obtaining the court's authority to act for the estate, so banks, title companies and other institutions will deal with you.

covers.title: Inventory and valuation
covers.text: Identifying and valuing real estate, accounts, business interests, vehicles, personal property and mineral rights. Texas law generally requires an inventory of the estate's assets unless an alternative filing is permitted.

covers.title: Debts, creditor claims and expenses
covers.text: Working out which funeral costs, medical bills, mortgages, card balances and taxes are legally valid claims against the estate.

covers.title: Distributing the estate
covers.text: Transferring real property and what remains under the terms of the will, or under Texas intestate succession law when there is none.

questions.q: Does every estate go through probate?
questions.a: No. Whether probate is necessary depends on whether property was owned solely in the deceased person's name, whether a valid will exists, how accounts are titled, whether assets have named beneficiaries or sit in a trust, and the size of the estate.

questions.q: How long does probate take in Texas?
questions.a: Some estates can be administered in a matter of months, while others take longer, depending on the assets, whether there is a will and whether disputes arise.

questions.q: How much does probate cost?
questions.a: It varies with the size of the estate, court filing fees, the complexity of the legal issues, whether disputes arise and the amount of work required. Michael West can discuss the anticipated costs during an initial consultation.

questions.q: Can probate be avoided?
questions.a: In some cases, yes, through revocable living trusts, beneficiary designations and transfer-on-death deeds put in place ahead of time.

questions.q: What does an executor do?
questions.a: Files the probate documents, protects the assets, notifies beneficiaries and creditors, pays valid debts, distributes what remains and closes the estate.

questions.q: What is the difference between an executor and an administrator?
questions.a: An executor is named in the will. An administrator is appointed by the court when there is no will, or when the person named cannot serve.

questions.q: Do I need a probate attorney?
questions.a: Texas law does not require legal representation in every probate matter, but most people choose to be represented.

questions.q: Can family members challenge a will?
questions.a: Yes, on grounds such as lack of testamentary capacity, undue influence, fraud, improper execution or forgery. Will contests involve strict legal standards and deadlines.

questions.q: What happens if there was no will?
questions.a: The person is said to have died intestate, and Texas law decides who inherits. The court appoints an administrator to do much of what an executor would have done.

services.title: Elder Law
services.summary: Long-term care, Medicaid and asset protection.
services.text: Elder law is a unique practice area encompassing many of the challenges and concerns of the elderly population in Texas. Whatever your situation may be, we can help you protect your rights and interests as you age.
services.lead: Michael West has built a focused elder law practice and completed specialized training at Elder Law College, working with aging clients and their families on care, assets and legacy across Pasadena, Houston, Harris County and the surrounding Texas communities.

covers.title: Medicaid planning
covers.text: Texas Medicaid rules are daunting. We help you preserve assets while legally qualifying for long-term care support, whether you are planning ahead or facing immediate nursing home costs.

covers.title: Medicare and healthcare advocacy
covers.text: Understanding what Medicare covers and what it does not, and putting medical powers of attorney, HIPAA releases and advance directives in place.

covers.title: Social Security and retirement benefits
covers.text: Applying for benefits, disputing a denial, and planning so you receive the retirement and disability benefits you have earned.

covers.title: Long-term care and assisted living planning
covers.text: Evaluating care options, reading facility contracts, and structuring finances to protect both the quality of care and the family's resources.

covers.title: Asset protection
covers.text: Structuring your holdings to shield them from litigation, liability and creditor claims, and protecting the family home from long-term care costs.

covers.title: Elder abuse prevention
covers.text: Intervening legally where elder abuse, neglect or financial exploitation is suspected, and using powers of attorney, trust planning and beneficiary reviews as safeguards.

covers.title: Legacy and inheritance
covers.text: Passing what you have built to the people and causes you choose.

questions.q: When should I speak with an elder law attorney?
questions.a: Before a crisis, if you can. Planning ahead gives you more options, whether you are thinking about nursing home costs, putting powers of attorney in place, updating an older plan after retirement, caring for an aging parent, or facing memory loss or cognitive decline.

services.title: Asset Protection
services.summary: Shielding assets from lawsuits and creditors.
services.text: Asset protection shields your hard-earned assets from risks such as lawsuits, creditors and unforeseen financial challenges.
services.lead: Asset protection is a vital aspect of securing your financial well-being. We craft tailored strategies to safeguard your wealth and provide peace of mind for you and your loved ones, and we integrate them into your overall estate plan.

covers.title: Asset protection trusts
covers.text: Irrevocable and other trusts used to shield assets from potential creditors and legal judgments.

covers.title: Limited liability entities
covers.text: LLCs, limited partnerships and corporations that separate business assets from personal assets.

covers.title: Homestead exemptions
covers.text: Using the Texas homestead exemption to protect your primary residence from creditors and certain legal claims.

covers.title: Insurance coverage
covers.text: Checking that liability insurance and umbrella policies are adequate for the risk you actually carry.

covers.title: Strategic planning
covers.text: Gifting, estate planning and retirement account strategies that preserve what you have built.

questions.q: Is asset protection legal?
questions.a: Yes. Asset protection planning uses legal strategies and structures within the bounds of the law to safeguard assets.

questions.q: When should I start?
questions.a: Proactively, and ideally before you face potential risks or liabilities.

questions.q: Can I protect all of my assets?
questions.a: These strategies shield many kinds of assets, but some are subject to specific legal requirements or limitations.

services.title: Guardianships
services.summary: Legal authority to care for a loved one.
services.text: Guardianships are legal arrangements in which a court appoints a guardian to make decisions on behalf of an individual who is unable to make decisions for themselves due to incapacity or disability.
services.lead: When an elderly or incapacitated loved one can no longer decide for themselves, guardianship gives a family member the legal authority to act. Guardianships are established for minors whose parents cannot care for them, and for adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities, mental illness or other conditions that impair their ability to decide independently.

covers.title: Guardianship of the person
covers.text: Authority over personal care, including healthcare, housing and education.

covers.title: Guardianship of the estate
covers.text: Authority to manage the ward's financial affairs, including assets, income and expenses.

covers.title: Limited and emergency guardianship
covers.text: Specific powers tailored to what the ward actually needs, preserving their rights as far as possible, and temporary authority where there is an immediate risk of harm.

covers.title: Petition and court proceedings
covers.text: Preparing and filing the petition for guardianship and representing you in court to establish it.

covers.title: Guardianship administration
covers.text: Ongoing guidance for the guardian on decisions, reporting requirements and legal obligations.

questions.q: Who can serve as a guardian?
questions.a: Family members, friends, professionals or organizations able to fulfil the responsibilities and act in the ward's best interests.

questions.q: Can guardianships be contested?
questions.a: Yes. Family members and others with an interest in the ward's well-being may contest a guardianship they believe is not in the ward's best interests.

questions.q: Can a guardianship be terminated or modified?
questions.a: Yes, if circumstances change or the guardianship is no longer necessary or appropriate for the ward's needs.

services.title: Special Needs Planning
services.summary: Trusts and benefits for a loved one with disabilities.
services.text: Helping families plan for the long-term well-being, security and care of loved ones with disabilities.
services.lead: A plan for a family member with disabilities has to provide for them without putting their benefits at risk. We build that plan and keep it current as circumstances change.

covers.title: Special needs trusts
covers.text: Setting money aside for a loved one while keeping means-tested benefits intact, so the trust can pay for education, therapy, travel and recreation.

covers.title: Government benefits navigation
covers.text: Evaluating eligibility and staying compliant with Medicaid, SSI, Medicare and other programs.

covers.title: Long-term financial planning
covers.text: A lasting strategy that folds in life insurance, retirement assets and public benefit considerations.

covers.title: Guardianship
covers.text: Guardianship petitions where a loved one needs someone with legal authority to decide for them.

services.title: Advance Directives
services.summary: Living wills, medical POAs and DNR orders.
services.text: Advance directives are essential legal documents that outline your healthcare preferences for a time when you cannot communicate your decisions yourself.
services.lead: Advance directives put your medical wishes in writing while you are able to express them, and name the person who speaks for you when you cannot.

covers.title: Living will
covers.text: A directive to physicians specifying the types of medical treatment you do or do not want if you are terminally ill or permanently unconscious.

covers.title: Healthcare proxy
covers.text: Also known as a medical power of attorney, it appoints someone to make healthcare decisions for you.

covers.title: Do not resuscitate order
covers.text: A DNR instructs healthcare providers not to perform CPR if your heart stops or you stop breathing.

covers.title: HIPAA authorization
covers.text: Lets your providers share medical information with the people you designate.

questions.q: Can I change my advance directives?
questions.a: Yes. You can update or revoke your advance directives at any time.

questions.q: Do I need a lawyer for this?
questions.a: Working with an experienced attorney ensures that your documents are legally sound.

questions.q: Who should I choose as my healthcare proxy?
questions.a: Select someone you trust who understands your values and wishes.

services.title: Prenuptial Agreements
services.text: Guidance for couples who want to set out how assets and responsibilities would be handled, with sensitivity and discretion.
services.lead: A prenuptial agreement sets out how assets and responsibilities would be handled in the event of divorce or death. It protects assets, makes financial expectations clear, encourages open conversation between partners, and can save time and legal fees later.

covers.title: What an agreement can cover
covers.text: Asset division, spousal support, inheritance rights and responsibility for debt.

covers.title: Sensitive and confidential service
covers.text: These agreements are handled with sensitivity and discretion, starting with a confidential consultation about your finances and goals.

covers.title: Review, negotiation and signing
covers.text: Drafting, review and negotiation, finalizing and signing, and ongoing support when the agreement needs updating.

questions.q: Do prenuptial agreements have to be one-sided?
questions.a: No. An agreement has to be fair and reasonable to be enforceable, and both parties should be able to review and negotiate the terms.

questions.q: Can a prenup be challenged in court?
questions.a: It is rare, but an agreement may be challenged if it was improperly executed, contains fraudulent information, or was signed under coercion.

questions.q: Can a prenup cover custody and child support?
questions.a: Generally no. Courts decide those matters based on the child's best interests.

services.title: Business Law
services.text: Whether you need help drawing up contracts or you need someone skilled in negotiation, or you need to bring litigation against someone, we've got you covered.
services.lead: West & West offers a wide variety of services to businesses of all sizes, with more than 40 years of combined experience in business and commercial litigation. We also help you structure your transactions and operations to minimize the potential for future litigation.

covers.title: Business formation and governance
covers.text: LLCs, corporations and partnerships, with operating agreements and bylaws written for your structure.

covers.title: Contracts
covers.text: Drafting and negotiating clear, enforceable contracts that protect your business relationships.

covers.title: Employment and non-compete agreements
covers.text: Safeguarding sensitive information, reducing employee-related risk, and handling wage and hour disputes.

covers.title: Intellectual property
covers.text: Patents, trademarks, copyrights and trade secrets, so the products, services and brand you built stay yours.

covers.title: Mergers and acquisitions
covers.text: Transfers of ownership, due diligence and regulatory compliance.

covers.title: Business disputes and litigation
covers.text: Partner and shareholder disputes, tortious interference, breach of fiduciary duty, unfair competition, deceptive business practices, insurance litigation and breach of contract.

covers.title: Dissolutions and liens
covers.text: Business dissolutions, and mechanics and materialman's liens.

covers.title: Succession planning
covers.text: Planning a smooth transition of ownership or management to the next generation or a buyer.

questions.q: Can you help before there is a dispute?
questions.a: Yes. Much of the work is structuring your transactions and operations to minimize the potential for future litigation.

services.title: Real Estate
services.text: Legal support for buying, selling, leasing and resolving disputes in both commercial and residential transactions.
services.lead: The firm's estate planning, probate and real estate team prepares deeds and handles commercial and residential transactions, including transfer on death and ladybird deeds.

covers.title: Residential transactions
covers.text: Buying, selling or refinancing single-family homes, condominiums and cooperative apartments.

covers.title: Commercial transactions
covers.text: Purchases, sales, leases and financing for office buildings, retail space, industrial property and mixed-use developments.

covers.title: Leasing
covers.text: Drafting and negotiating commercial leases for landlords and tenants, with clear terms and protections for both sides.

covers.title: Real estate development
covers.text: Land acquisition, zoning and land use approvals, construction contracts and project financing.

covers.title: Title examination and insurance
covers.text: Reviewing title reports, resolving title defects and obtaining title insurance against ownership disputes.

covers.title: Deeds
covers.text: Preparing deeds, including transfer on death and ladybird deeds.

covers.title: Property tax assessment appeals
covers.text: Challenging an unfair or excessive property tax assessment to reduce the liability.

questions.q: Do I need an attorney for a real estate transaction?
questions.a: Legal representation is not required for every transaction, but an attorney provides guidance and protection through the process.

questions.q: What is involved in the closing process?
questions.a: Executing the closing documents, paying closing costs and fees, and transferring ownership from the seller to the buyer. We represent you at the closing.

questions.q: How long does a real estate transaction take?
questions.a: It varies with the complexity of the transaction, the financing, any title issues and local regulations. We can estimate the timeline once we know the specifics.

process.title: How we work
process.text: The same approach whether the matter is an injury claim, a probate or an estate plan.

steps.title: You tell us what happened
steps.text: From the moment you contact the office, we take the time to understand your situation and answer your questions.

steps.title: We explain your options
steps.text: Your rights, your options and the legal process, set out in plain, honest language.

steps.title: We build the strategy
steps.text: No two legal matters are alike, so the plan is built around your circumstances and goals.

steps.title: We walk it through with you
steps.text: You are never left guessing about the next step, from the first consultation to the resolution of your case.

about.title: A multigenerational family practice in Pasadena.
text: Some law firms are built around numbers. Ours was built around people, and family. West & West, LLP is a multigenerational law practice rooted in integrity, personal attention and a deep commitment to helping our community through life's most challenging legal moments.

As a locally owned law firm, we see every client as a neighbor. Our principal attorney, Michael West, leads the firm. His wife, Laura West, serves as business manager and mediation coordinator. The West family legacy in law does not stop there: Michael's father, the Honorable David West, served as a Harris County judge for 13 years, from 1984 to 1997, and was Michael's law partner for more than two decades.

Because we are quite literally a family in law, we take a family-first approach to how we treat our clients. When you hire us, we treat your case with the same care and dedication we would give our own loved ones.

values.title: Educating our clients
values.text: When you come to our law firm, we won't just tell you what your case is, we'll teach it to you. We make sure you understand every aspect of your situation before you walk out our doors.

values.title: Fighting for community
values.text: You're a part of our community just as much as us. We take care of our people and we want to be involved in serving them as much as possible.

values.title: Relationships over transactions
values.text: We'll never pressure you into a course of action that benefits us more than it benefits you, and we'll explain your options thoroughly before you decide.

team.name: Michael West
team.bio: Michael is the principal attorney and has devoted over 30 years to the practice of law, continuing the family legacy begun by his father, the late retired State District Judge David West, who was his law partner for more than two decades. "Working with my father taught me many lessons," he says, "and the most important is to look out for your clients first." He began his practice in downtown Houston and moved the office to Pasadena to be closer to his clients. He holds a Doctor of Jurisprudence from South Texas College of Law and a BBA in finance and economics from Baylor University, and completed 40-hour mediation training at the A.A. White Dispute Resolution Institute. Most of his career has been spent representing individuals in personal injury and wrongful death, auto and truck accidents, workplace injuries and other negligence claims, and more recently in elder law.

team.name: Laura West
team.bio: Laura came in to help for two weeks and stayed more than a decade. As business manager and mediation coordinator she prepares wills and probate documents, manages invoices and payments, and keeps the firm running. Her favorite part of the job is meeting new clients and putting people at ease. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in business administration from Baylor University, takes part in Bible Study Fellowship and serves as Sunday School director at South Main Baptist Church. She is a mother of three and a grandmother of two.

team.name: Sonia Emmons
team.bio: Sonia is part of the estate planning, probate and real estate team, assisting with wills, probates and deeds. By day she is a school bus driver, and she brings the same care, precision and calm to legal documents as she does to her route.

faqs.q: How do I meet with the attorney?
faqs.a: Michael West meets clients at the Pasadena office or over Zoom, and offers after-hours and in-home consultations when they are needed. Clients work directly with him rather than through a series of case managers or call centers.

faqs.q: What does a personal injury case cost up front?
faqs.a: Consultations are free and carry no obligation, the firm works on a contingency fee basis, and there are no attorney fees unless we win your case. You can call 24/7.

faqs.q: Do you only take cases in Pasadena?
faqs.a: No. The firm represents clients across Pasadena, Houston, Deer Park, La Porte and the surrounding areas of Harris County, and in communities throughout Southeast Texas.

faqs.q: How long do I have to bring an injury claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Generally two years from the date of the injury, and some claims have shorter deadlines. Texas law often imposes strict time limits for filing claims.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to settle a relative's estate?
faqs.a: Not every estate requires formal probate, and simplified procedures are sometimes available under Texas law. Working out which process applies is usually the first step.

faqs.q: How often should I review my estate plan?
faqs.a: After any major life event, and otherwise every three to five years is a good practice.

faqs.q: Will I understand what is happening in my case?
faqs.a: That is the point. When you come to the firm, we won't just tell you what your case is, we'll teach it to you, so you understand every aspect of your situation.
